reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A keloid is firm, rubbery, and shiny, and crucially extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, distinguishing it from a hypertrophic scar that stays within the wound margins
Lesions often itch or feel tender and may continue to enlarge over months to years rather than regressing
Predilection sites include the earlobes, presternal chest, shoulders, upper back, and jawline
Risk is higher in people with darker skin phototypes, in younger patients, and where there is a family history
Even minor triggers such as ear piercing, acne, vaccination, or surgery can precipitate lesions in predisposed individuals
Prevention matters: minimise tension on wounds, avoid unnecessary elective procedures in prone sites, and counsel high-risk patients before piercings or cosmetic surgery
Treatment is often multimodal and includes intralesional anti-inflammatory injection, pressure or silicone therapy, and carefully planned surgery combined with adjuvant measures to reduce recurrence
Surgical excision alone carries a high recurrence rate and can produce a larger keloid, so it should be paired with adjuvant therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Keloids arise from dysregulated wound healing in which the normal resolution of the proliferative phase fails and fibroblasts remain persistently activated. Overexpression of profibrotic mediators, notably transforming growth factor-beta, drives excessive and disorganised deposition of thick, hyalinised collagen bundles that extend into surrounding normal dermis. Reduced apoptosis of fibroblasts, altered mechanotransduction from wound tension, and a genetic predisposition all contribute. Unlike hypertrophic scars, keloids do not remodel and regress over time, reflecting a sustained imbalance between collagen synthesis and breakdown.
additionalDifferentials: Hypertrophic scar (raised but confined to the wound edges and tends to regress)
Cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis in a scar
Nodular presentation of acne keloidalis nuchae on the occipital scalp
additionalInvestigations: Diagnosis is clinical based on history and morphology
Skin biopsy only when an alternative or malignant process is suspected, recognising that biopsy itself may stimulate keloid growth
Photographic documentation to monitor size and response to treatment
redFlags: Rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding, or fixation suggesting a fibrosarcomatous tumour rather than a keloid
Recurrent or aggressive lesions in a scar raising the possibility of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans
Functional impairment or contracture over a joint or the ear requiring specialist input
reference.prognosis: Keloids are chronic and prone to recurrence; some stabilise with combined therapy, but complete and permanent resolution is difficult, and lesions frequently recur after excision unless adjuvant treatment is used. They do not spontaneously involute in the way hypertrophic scars often do.
pitfalls: Excising a keloid without adjuvant therapy, which commonly produces a larger recurrence
Failing to distinguish a keloid from a self-limiting hypertrophic scar and over-treating
Performing elective cosmetic procedures or piercings in high-risk patients without counselling
Overlooking the symptom burden of itch and pain and treating only for appearance
